card.title: Preparing the breach records
card.question: Which incident records can we trust and use, and in what form, to learn how breaches happen?

variables.name: employee_count
variables.transform: ordered levels, Unknown kept as level

variables.name: size
variables.transform: ordered levels, Unknown kept as level

prep_steps: Read 10596 validated incident files and flattened each into one row of 53 fields plus two ids
Mapped the first two NAICS digits to the Census 2022 sector name
Grouped employee counts into small (up to 100, or VERIS Small), medium (101 to 1000), large
Kept Unknown as its own category instead of filling it in
Took log10(1 + records lost) for the 5398 incidents with a known count
Breach target: Yes is 1; No, or no confidentiality section at all, is 0 (VERIS records that section only when data was affected); Potentially and Unknown dropped, leaving 8267 incidents

sample_rows.sector: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing

card.why: Records lost is extremely right skewed (skewness 50.6): the mean is 22,774,208 while the median is 1,364, so a few mega breaches dominate any raw average. After log10(1 + x) the skewness falls to 0.36, which makes regression and distance based methods usable. Dropping every row with any gap would remove 98% of incidents, so Unknown is kept as a category and only each model's own inputs must be present.

data_properties.name: Skewness of records lost (raw)
data_properties.implication: A few huge breaches dominate; raw averages and linear fits would be misleading.

data_properties.name: Skewness of log10(1 + records lost)
data_properties.implication: Close to symmetric, so the log scale is used for every model of breach size.

data_properties.name: IQR outliers in records lost, raw then log
data_properties.implication: The log scale turns most extreme values into ordinary ones, so none are deleted.

data_properties.name: Share of breach target that is Yes
data_properties.implication: Very unbalanced classes: accuracy is meaningless, use ROC AUC and class weights.

data_properties.name: Rows with at least one missing or Unknown field
data_properties.implication: Listwise deletion would throw away most of the data.

alternatives.why_not: The mean (22,774,208) is far above the median (1,364) because of skewness 50.6, so filling gaps with it would invent huge breaches.
It would drop 10334 of 10596 incidents (98%), mostly because Unknown is common.

alternatives.model: Treating Potentially as Yes for the target
alternatives.why_not: 2109 incidents say only Potentially; counting them as breaches would mix confirmed and suspected losses.

assumptions.check: Normality of log10(1 + records lost), D'Agostino K squared
assumptions.action_taken: Keep log scale for symmetry; later models use tests robust to non-normality where needed.

charts.title: Records lost on the log scale

card.yields: Out of 10596 public incident reports, 8267 clearly say whether data was exposed and 5398 say how many records were lost. CyCRS learns how breaches happen from these rows and measures breach size on a log scale so one giant leak does not distort the picture for a small business.
limitations: Only 775 incidents (9.4%) are No, so the breach classifier still has far fewer negatives than positives.
688 incidents have no confidentiality section and are counted as no disclosure; this assumes the coder would have recorded any data exposure.

card.yields: A typical breach in the data exposes about 1,364 records and goes unnoticed for about 91 days, while a few huge breaches pull the average up to 22,774,208. Hacking is the most common kind of attack and outsiders cause most incidents, so CyCRS starts its threat list there.

card.title: Which curve fits breach size
card.question: Is the number of records lost in a breach closer to a normal or a lognormal distribution?

data_in.dataset: VCDB validated incidents with a known record count

variables.name: data_total
variables.transform: none for the fit, ln for the QQ plot

prep_steps: Kept incidents with data_total known (all values are at least 1)
Fitted both distributions by maximum likelihood, lognormal location fixed at 0

card.why: Records lost is strictly positive with skewness 50.6, the typical shape of a lognormal variable, while a normal curve allows negative values and is symmetric. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance is 0.486 for the normal fit and 0.091 for the lognormal fit, so the lognormal curve is much closer to the data.

data_properties.name: KS D, normal fit
data_properties.implication: Large gap between data and normal curve.

data_properties.name: KS D, lognormal fit
data_properties.implication: Much smaller gap; log scale is appropriate.

data_properties.name: Lognormal sigma (shape)
data_properties.implication: Wide spread on the log scale.

data_properties.name: Lognormal median (scale)
data_properties.implication: Typical breach size implied by the fit.

alternatives.why_not: KS D 0.486; it predicts negative record counts and misses the long tail.
Describes only the largest breaches; CyCRS needs the whole range, including small breaches.

assumptions.action_taken: Normal model not used for breach size.
With n this large even small gaps are significant; D is used to compare fits and the log scale is adopted.

card.yields: Breach sizes follow a lognormal pattern far better than a bell curve (distance 0.091 vs 0.486). That is why every later model of breach size in CyCRS works on the log of records lost and converts back to records and rupees at the end.
limitations: KS p-values are optimistic because parameters were estimated from the same data.
Even the lognormal fit is rejected at this sample size; it is an approximation, not an exact law.

card.title: Attack chances by sector
card.question: Given a business's sector, what share of past incidents involved each kind of attack?

data_in.dataset: VCDB validated incidents in the top 8 sectors
prep_steps: Kept incidents in the 8 most common known sectors
Each probability is the share of that sector's incidents with the action flag set

sample_rows.sector: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing

card.why: Sector and action category are both categorical, so the simplest honest estimate of P(action | sector) is the observed share within each sector. Every top sector has at least 271 incidents, enough for stable shares, and the chi-square test finds attack mix depends on sector (Cramer's V 0.25).

data_properties.name: Smallest sector sample
data_properties.implication: Shares are estimated from at least this many incidents.

data_properties.name: Top attack in Health Care and Social Assistance
data_properties.implication: Leading threat for the largest sector.

data_properties.name: Cramer's V, action vs sector
data_properties.implication: Sector changes the attack mix.

alternatives.model: One overall attack mix for everyone
alternatives.why_not: The chi-square test rejects independence (p 0), so ignoring sector loses information.
Used later for the live model; this table is the transparent reference it must beat.

assumptions.action_taken: No smoothing needed for the top 8 sectors.

card.yields: In Health Care and Social Assistance, 27% of past incidents involved physical, and each sector has its own leading threat. CyCRS shows these shares as the simple baseline for a user's sector, and its attack likelihood model must do better than this table to be used.
limitations: An incident can have several action categories, so a sector's shares can add up to more than 1.
Shares describe reported incidents, not the chance that a given business is attacked.

card.title: Testing what really differs
card.question: Which differences in attack type, breach size, detection time and regional crime are real rather than chance?

data_in.dataset: VCDB validated incidents and NCRB Crime in India 2024 state tables
prep_steps: Primary action is the single action category, or multiple; unknown dropped for chi-square tests
Action rows with fewer than 5 incidents dropped from contingency tables
Internal vs external compares incidents with only one actor class
States and UTs grouped into five regions by CyCRS (Chhattisgarh in East, Madhya Pradesh in West)
Holm correction applied across all tests in the table

card.why: Normality checks fail for breach size (internal p 2.1e-42) and for log discovery time (p 3.6e-15), so rank-based tests (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis) are primary. Attack type, size and sector are categorical, so association is tested with chi-square and sized with Cramer's V, and ransomware share is a proportion, so a two-proportion z-test fits. Running 9 tests raises the chance of a false alarm, so Holm-adjusted p-values decide.

data_properties.name: Shapiro-Wilk p, log records lost, internal
data_properties.implication: Not normal: use a rank test.

data_properties.name: Shapiro-Wilk p, log discovery days
data_properties.implication: Not normal: Kruskal-Wallis is primary.

data_properties.name: Levene p, discovery days by sector
data_properties.implication: Unequal spreads also weaken ANOVA.

data_properties.name: Tests rejected after Holm
data_properties.implication: Number of differences treated as real.

alternatives.why_not: Assumes normal data; Shapiro-Wilk rejects normality even after the log transform.

alternatives.model: One-way ANOVA as primary test for discovery time
alternatives.why_not: Normality and equal variance fail (Levene p 1.5e-09); ANOVA is kept only as a comparison row.
Expected counts are large (minimum 0.2), so chi-square is accurate and Fisher is unnecessary.

assumptions.action_taken: Mann-Whitney U instead of t-test.

card.yields: 7 of 9 tested differences hold up after correcting for multiple tests: attack mix by business size, attack mix by sector, breach size by insider or outsider, detection time by sector (ANOVA), the rise in ransomware share, the ransomware rise without 2023, crime type mix by Indian region, while detection time by sector (Kruskal-Wallis), crime rate by Indian region could be chance. CyCRS uses only the differences that survive as inputs for tailoring its advice, and shows the effect size so a statistically real but tiny difference is not oversold.
limitations: VCDB is not a random sample of businesses, so tests describe reported incidents.
With thousands of incidents even negligible differences can be significant; read the effect size.
The five-region grouping of states is a CyCRS choice and affects the regional tests.
857 incidents are dated 2023 and 91% of them involve ransomware; without them the share from 2020 is 22.1% instead of 55.2% (robustness row), so part of the rise is a collection effect.

Placed each band at its geometric midpoint; Over 100000 at its lower bound

card.why: Both variables are on log scales, where breach size is close to symmetric (skewness 0.36), so a straight line is a fair first model. A single predictor shows how much size alone explains before adding attack details; here R2 is 0.117.

Used next; this single-predictor model is the baseline it must improve on.

assumptions.action_taken: Size kept as a predictor in the multiple model.

card.yields: Each tenfold increase in staff cuts expected records lost to about 30% (larger organisations in VCDB tend to lose fewer records), but size alone explains only 11.7% of the variation. So CyCRS does not judge breach size from company size alone; it adds sector and attack type in the multiple model.

Large organisations dominate VCDB.

title: Which incidents end in data loss

card.title: Which incidents end in data loss
card.module: 4: Classification (logistic regression, decision tree, KNN, Naive Bayes, LDA, ROC, confusion matrix)
card.question: Can the kind of attack, attacker and assets involved tell us whether an incident ends in confirmed data disclosure?

data_in.dataset: VCDB incidents with data_disclosure Yes or No
prep_steps: Stratified 70/30 split (random_state 42): train 5244 Yes / 542 No, test 2248 Yes / 233 No
Dropped flags that, in the training rows, occur in only one class or fewer than 5 times: action_environmental
Standard scaling inside the pipeline for logistic, KNN and LDA; class_weight balanced for logistic and tree
asset_person left out: VERIS codes the targeted person as an asset in every social attack, so it restates the label

card.why: The target is binary and only 9.4% of training incidents are No, so models are compared on AUC and recall/specificity rather than accuracy, and class weights are used where supported. Each model has a data-based reason: logistic, binary target with 24 binary predictors; class weights offset the 542 No cases in training; decision_tree, finds interactions between attack and asset flags as readable rules; depth 10 and leaf 20 chosen by CV AUC; knn, non-parametric baseline on scaled flags; k = 2 minimised CV balanced error; naive_bayes, all predictors are 0/1 flags, so Bernoulli Naive Bayes is the matching likelihood; lda, linear boundary with shared covariance; a classical comparison for logistic regression.

data_properties.name: Share of No in training
data_properties.implication: Severe imbalance: accuracy is misleading.

data_properties.name: No cases in test set
data_properties.implication: Test AUC and specificity are estimated from very few cases.

data_properties.name: Best model by CV AUC
data_properties.implication: Model used for the Youden threshold.

data_properties.name: Youden threshold for best model
data_properties.implication: J = 0.555; balances recall and specificity.

alternatives.why_not: Predicting Yes for every incident already scores 0.906 accuracy.
Synthesising 542 rare cases of binary flags creates unrealistic incidents; class weights are simpler and in the syllabus.

assumptions.action_taken: Class weights, AUC-based selection, Youden threshold.
Odds ratios read from the statsmodels fit.

card.yields: Decision tree separates data-loss incidents best (CV AUC 0.83), and the strongest logistic signals are action_physical (odds ratio 5.15), sector_health_care_and_social_assistance (odds ratio 4.97), action_error (odds ratio 4.26). With only 542 No cases to learn from, CyCRS treats most incidents as likely to expose data and uses this model only to explain which attack features matter, not to promise a business it is safe.
limitations: Only 775 incidents are confirmed No, so every No-side metric is uncertain.
Potentially and Unknown disclosures were dropped; incidents with no confidentiality section count as No, which assumes VERIS coders recorded every exposure.
CV AUC SD for the best model is 0.019, so model ranks may change with a new sample.

title: How many things really describe an incident

card.title: How many things really describe an incident
card.question: How many independent dimensions are hidden in the dozens of yes/no flags that describe each incident?

prep_steps: Used 37 0/1 incident flags with non-zero variance
Standardised each flag to mean 0, SD 1 before PCA

card.why: The 37 flags overlap heavily (a ransomware flag implies a malware flag, an error flag often comes with media assets), so PCA can compress them into a few uncorrelated components. Kaiser's rule keeps 12 components and 80% of the variance needs 14, which measures how much redundancy there is.

data_properties.name: Components with eigenvalue above 1
data_properties.implication: Kaiser dimension count.

data_properties.name: Components for 80% variance
data_properties.implication: Dimensions needed to keep most information.

data_properties.name: Variance explained by PC1
data_properties.implication: +action_hacking / +actor_external

data_properties.name: Variance explained by PC2
data_properties.implication: +action_social / +asset_person

alternatives.why_not: Flags are binary and FA assumes continuous, roughly normal indicators; it is used on NCRB rates instead.
PC1 and PC2 alone carry 29% of the variance, so plots and clustering on raw flags would be noisy.

assumptions.action_taken: First 8 components interpreted.

card.yields: The 37 incident flags boil down to about 12 independent patterns by Kaiser's rule (14 to keep 80% of the information), led by +action_hacking / +actor_external. That is 32% as many dimensions as flags, so the flags overlap but each still adds information; CyCRS keeps the separate attack categories rather than replacing them with components.
limitations: PCA on binary flags is descriptive; components are linear summaries, not causal factors.
Rare flags get large standardised values and can dominate later components.

card.title: Business personas

k chosen by the highest mean silhouette over k = 2 to 10

K-means suits this because assignment is a simple distance to 8 saved centres, and the silhouette peaks at k = 8 (0.29).

card.title: Checking the personas another way
card.question: Does a different clustering method find the same business personas?

prep_steps: Random sample of 500 incidents because Ward linkage needs all pairwise distances
Tree cut at k = 8

card.why: Ward linkage merges the pair of groups that least increases within-group variance, the same quantity K-means minimises, so agreement between the two is a fair test of persona stability. The adjusted Rand index between the two labelings is 0.44, where 1 is identical and 0 is chance.

data_properties.name: Adjusted Rand index vs K-means
data_properties.implication: Personas are partly stable.

alternatives.why_not: On 0/1 data with many tied distances they chain or produce one giant cluster; Ward matches the K-means objective.
10596 incidents need about 56,137,608 distances; a 500-row sample is enough to test stability.

assumptions.action_taken: Reported with the personas.

card.yields: An independent method only partly recovers the personas (adjusted Rand index 0.44), so their broad shape is real but the exact boundaries depend on the algorithm. CyCRS uses them for instant assignment and presents them as rough groupings.
limitations: Based on a 500-row sample.
Many identical 0/1 profiles create tied distances.

card.yields: On 3105 unseen incidents, CyCRS's top 3 controls addressed what happened 20.9% of the time, against 20.9% for the fixed baseline (p 1). Most misses are attacks like errors and misuse whose controls cannot be scored yet, which is where sourcing more effectiveness data would help most.
limitations: VCDB incidents are not Indian small businesses.
Hit means the control addresses the attack type, not that it would have stopped it.
